questions.question: From the Persian 'pae-jamah' meaning 'leg-garment', and picked up by the British in colonial India, comes which English word for soft sleepwear?
questions.explanation: Persian pae (leg) + jamah (garment); entered English from Hindi via British India around 1800.

questions.question: Our English word 'paradise' comes from an Old Persian word, 'pairidaeza'. What did 'pairidaeza' literally mean?
questions.explanation: Avestan pairi- (around) + diz (to make a wall); travelled through Greek paradeisos to English.

questions.question: Chess came to Europe from India via Persia. Our word 'checkmate' is a worn-down version of the Persian 'shah mat'. What does 'shah mat' literally mean?
questions.explanation: Persian shah (king) + mat (helpless, astonished); often retold as 'the king is dead'.

questions.question: From the Persian 'bazar' meaning 'a market', comes which English word for a busy marketplace or a charity fundraiser stall?
questions.explanation: From Persian bazar (market), via Italian bazarra, into English in the 1580s.

questions.question: From the Persian 'karwan' meaning 'a group of desert travellers', comes which English word now used for both a procession of vehicles and a holiday trailer?
questions.explanation: Persian karwan, picked up during the Crusades via Arabic qairawan.

questions.question: When British army officers in India wanted a dust-coloured uniform that wouldn't show dirt, they borrowed the Persian word for 'dust' itself. What English word for a brownish-yellow colour did this give us?
questions.explanation: From Urdu khaki ('dusty'), from Persian khak ('dust'); adopted for uniforms around 1857.

questions.question: From the Persian 'kushk' meaning a pavilion or summer house, comes which English word now used for a small street stall selling newspapers or a touch-screen ordering booth?
questions.explanation: Persian kushk to Turkish koshk to French kiosque; arrived in English in the 1620s.

questions.question: From the Arabic root 'shariba' meaning 'he drank' — via Persian 'sharbat' (a drink) and Turkish 'serbet' — comes which English word for a fruity frozen dessert?
questions.explanation: Arabic shariba ('he drank') gave Persian sharbat and Turkish serbet; English from the 1580s. Also gave us 'syrup' and 'sorbet'.

questions.question: Our English word 'julep' comes from the Persian 'gulab'. What does 'gulab' literally mean? (Hint: 'gul' is a flower, 'ab' is water.)
questions.explanation: Persian gul (rose) + ab (water); entered medical Latin as a syrupy medicine, later a minty drink.

questions.question: From the Persian 'shal' (possibly named after a town in India where it was first made), comes which English word for a long piece of cloth worn around the shoulders?
questions.explanation: Persian shal, possibly from Shaliat in India; English from the 1660s.

questions.question: From the Persian 'pistah', through Greek and Italian, comes which English word for a green nut often used in ice cream and baklava?
questions.explanation: Persian pistah, via Greek pistakion and Italian pistacchio; English from the 1590s.

questions.question: From the Persian 'aspanakh', through Arabic and Spanish, comes which English word for the leafy green Popeye is famous for eating?
questions.explanation: Persian aspanakh -> Arabic isbanakh / Andalusian isbinakh -> Catalan/Provencal espinac/espinarc -> Old French espinache -> English by the late 13th century.

questions.question: From Sanskrit, through Persian 'narang' and Arabic 'naranj', comes which English word for a sweet citrus fruit? (The leading 'n' got eaten by a confused definite article along the way.)
questions.explanation: Sanskrit naranga to Persian narang to Arabic naranj to Italian arancia; n- lost via confusion with articles.

questions.question: From Sanskrit 'khanda' for a piece of sugar, through Persian 'qand' and Arabic 'qandi', we get the English word for sweets. What is it?
questions.explanation: Sanskrit khanda to Persian qand (cane sugar) to Arabic qandi to Old French sucre candi.

questions.question: From the Arabic 'al-jabr', meaning roughly 'the reunion of broken parts', and from a 9th-century treatise by the Baghdad mathematician al-Khwarizmi, comes which English word that strikes fear into school students everywhere?
questions.explanation: From al-Khwarizmi's treatise on al-jabr wa al-muqabala (restoring and balancing).

questions.question: The same 9th-century Baghdad mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose name means 'native of Khwarazm', gave his name, in a mangled Latin form, to which modern English word now central to computing?
questions.explanation: Medieval Latin algorismus, a garbled transliteration of al-Khwarizmi's name.

questions.question: Our English word 'alcohol' comes from the Arabic 'al-kuhul'. What did 'al-kuhul' originally mean?
questions.answer: A fine powder (kohl, used as eye make-up)
questions.explanation: Arabic al-kuhul meant the powdered antimony used as eye cosmetic; the meaning broadened to 'pure spirit of anything'.

questions.question: From the Arabic 'sifr', meaning 'empty' or 'nothing' (itself a translation of the Sanskrit 'shunya'), come two English words. One means 'a secret code'. What's the other, more numerical one?
questions.explanation: Arabic sifr gave English both 'zero' and 'cipher'; the Arabs translated the Sanskrit concept shunya.

questions.question: From the Arabic 'makhazin' meaning 'storehouses', comes which English word now used both for a periodical you read on the beach and for the part of a gun that holds bullets?
questions.explanation: Arabic makhazin (plural of makhzan, 'storehouse'), via Italian and French.

questions.question: From the Arabic 'suffah' meaning a bench of stone or wood with cushions, comes which English word for the long soft seat in your living room?
questions.explanation: Arabic suffah ('bench, couch'), via Turkish, in English from the 1620s.

questions.question: From the Arabic 'hashishin', the name Europeans gave to a particular Nizari Ismaili sect during the Crusades, comes which English word for someone who murders an important person?
questions.explanation: Arabic hashishin, name for the Nizari Ismaili sect; English from the 1530s via Italian.

questions.question: From the Hindi verb 'champna' meaning 'to press or knead the muscles' (the imperative is 'champo'), comes which English word now found on every bottle in your bathroom?
questions.explanation: Originally meant therapeutic head/body massage in Anglo-Indian English (1762); shifted to hair-washing by 1860.

questions.question: From the Hindi 'bangla', literally meaning 'in the style of Bengal', referring to a low thatched house with a verandah, comes which English word for a single-storey house?
questions.explanation: Hindi bangla via Gujarati bangalo; in Anglo-Indian use from the 1670s.

questions.question: From Hindi 'Jagannath', a title of Krishna meaning 'lord of the world', and the huge chariot at Puri that bears his image in procession, comes which English word for an unstoppable, crushing force?
questions.explanation: Sanskrit jagat (the world) + natha (lord); from the Puri chariot procession.

questions.question: From the Hindi 'lut' meaning 'to plunder', comes which short English word for stolen goods?
questions.explanation: Hindi lut, from Sanskrit loptram ('booty'); entered English from Anglo-Indian usage in 1802.

questions.question: From the Hindi 'thag' meaning a cheat or swindler, and the gangs of stranglers and robbers in India whom the British suppressed in the 1830s, comes which English word for a violent ruffian?
questions.explanation: Hindi/Marathi thag; the meaning generalised from the Indian gangs to any cutthroat by 1839.

questions.question: From the Tamil 'kattu-maram', literally 'tied wood', comes which English word for a boat with two parallel hulls?
questions.explanation: Tamil kattu (to tie) + maram (wood, tree); English from the 1670s.

questions.question: Named after the Indian seaport of Calicut, now called Kozhikode, on the Malabar coast, comes which English word for a printed cotton cloth?
questions.explanation: From Calicut, an alternative form of the port-city name; English from the 1530s.

questions.question: Named after the city in northern Iraq where it was made, comes which English word for a fine, lightweight cotton fabric?
questions.explanation: From Italian Mussolo, the Italian name for Mosul; English from around 1600.

questions.question: From the Turkish 'ordu' meaning 'a camp or army' (the same word that gives the name of a language spoken in Pakistan), comes which English word for a vast, unruly crowd?
questions.explanation: Tatar urda / Turkish ordu ('camp, army'); same root gives the language name Urdu.
